text.p: France's Sommer Allibert defended a plan to merge its floor-covering business, including Canadian vinyl flooring firm Domco, with Tarkett AG of Germany, and reiterated on Thursday that it would not tender its Domco shares to a bid by Armstrong World Industries.
The French group accused U.S.-based Armstrong of misleading shareholders through inappropriate comparisons of its bid and the Sommer-Tarkett deal in an open letter to Armstrong chairman George Lorch.

U.S.-based Armstrong filed suits in Canada and the United States this week against Domco's directors and Sommer Allibert, which holds 69.2 percent of Domco, accusign them of disregarding the rights of minority shareholders by rejecting its buyout offer of C$23 per share, or C$488 million.
In an interview with the French newspaper Les Echos, Lorch said Domco's shareholders all stood to benefit from Armstrong's bid, which represents a 56 percent premium on the stock.

"Even Sommer Allibert -- which could gain more than one billion francs from the sale, a sum that could be useful in helping it reduce its debt and develop its main activity, auto parts," Lorch was quoted as saying.
He said Domco's directors had the obligation not to subordinate the interests of their minority shareholders to those of major stockholder Sommer Allibert.

He said one of Sommer Allibert's U.S. shareholders, Wyser-Pratte which holds three percent along with its French subsidiary Verneuil Finance, was in favour of Armstrong's bid for Domco. "I don't think you can ignore shareholders' interests for very long, be they Domco's or Sommer Allibert's," he said.

Sommer Allibert reached an agreement in May to merge its floor-covering businesses, including Domco, with Tarkett in a 1.36 billion mark deal creating the world's leading producer of floor coverings after rejecting Armstrong's offer to buy its floor and wall covering businesses.
Sommer Allibert said in a statement that the group's decision to strengthen its second core business "should allow us to improve our performance".

In an open letter to Armstrong's boss, Sommer Allibert Chairman said he was convinced that the decision to create a world leader in floor and wall coverings with Tarkett "was, and remains, in the best interest of all our shareholders".
He said the group had at no time agreed to negotiate exclusively with Armstrong, referring to the talks between the two companies over the past year that had led to Armstrong's offer in April.
In the letter, a reply to one from Lorch, he also denied Armstrong's accusation that the French company had violated any confidentiality agreement.
